title: AI Consulting Cost in 2026: 4 Tiers, From €2,500 to €300,000
excerpt: AI consulting cost in 2026 splits into four real tiers, from €2,500 workshops to €300K enterprise programs. Here is what each price actually delivers, what hides inside the spread, and how to scope your engagement to the tier that fits.
metaDescription: AI consulting cost in 2026 splits into four real tiers, from €2,500 workshops to €300K enterprise programs. What each delivers and how to pick yours.

blocks.text: **AI consulting in 2026 costs €2,500 to €300,000+** across four honest tiers: workshops, AI readiness audits, pilot builds, and enterprise AI programs. The 100x spread is real because each tier is a different deliverable shape with a different team, not the same engagement at different markups.

Everyone says AI consulting is expensive. The data says most buyers pay €40,000 for a 60-page slide deck that should have been a €5,000 workshop, or €8,000 for a strategy review that should have been a €60,000 production pilot.

You are looking at three AI consulting proposals: €4,500 from a freelancer, €38,000 from a boutique studio, €175,000 from a Big 4 practice. All claim to solve the same problem. The math seems broken because nobody publishes what each price actually buys.
This guide names the four real tiers in 2026, what hides inside each price, and the four filters that scope your engagement to the tier that fits.

items: **Four real tiers in 2026.** Workshops (€1,500 to €5K, 1 week), AI readiness audits with roadmap (€2,500 to €25K, 2 to 4 weeks), pilot builds with working code (€25K to €75K, 4 to 10 weeks), enterprise AI programs (€75K to €300K+, 12 to 26 weeks).
**Tier confusion drives most wasted spend.** Buying a slide deck when you needed a pilot, or an enterprise program when a one-day workshop would have answered the question.

**Inside each tier, deliverable depth drives the spread.** Engineer-hours versus analyst-hours, production code versus PowerPoint, founder access versus junior associate, working architecture versus a recommendation slide.

**The €60K slide deck is the most common AI consulting trap.** A multi-page roadmap from a consultancy that has never shipped an LLM workflow into production costs the same as a working pilot from an engineering-led shop.

blocks.text: The Price Spread Is Real, And It Is Not Agency Markup

Three things drive the spread. First, what is actually inside the deliverable. A one-day workshop with an engineer who ships LLMs daily produces different output than a six-month engagement with a junior associate writing a roadmap from public sources.

Second, who sits in the meeting. The Big 4 quote includes a partner for one kickoff call and an analyst pool for the rest. A boutique with a working engineer in the room costs a third as much because the analyst pool was never the value.

Third, what the engagement produces. A slide deck has near-zero handover cost and near-zero production value. A working pilot has every line of code in your repository on day one. The price reflects the artifact, not the brand.

[Anthropic's $1.5B consulting joint venture with Wall Street](/blog/ai-labs-services-distribution) in early 2026 set the ceiling. Frontier AI labs are entering services because consulting capacity is the real bottleneck in enterprise AI adoption. The new ceiling is real, and so is the new floor: a workshop with a working engineer now costs less than most teams pay for a Notion seat upgrade.
The 4 AI Consulting Tiers in 2026

Each tier is a different deliverable shape with a different team and a different timeline. The tier you actually need depends on what production state you are in, not how many AI vendors you have evaluated.

blocks.text: Tier 1: Workshops and Advisory Days (€1,500 to €5K, 1 week)

A focused session with an engineer who builds LLM systems in production. Typical scope: one or two days of workshops, a written summary of the right next step, and a short Q&A follow-up. Replaces six weeks of internal debate about whether AI fits your problem.

items: **Who it is for:** teams who have read three AI strategy articles and need one hour with someone who has shipped the thing, not someone who has read about it.
**What you get:** a clear answer on whether your use case is AI-shaped or not, the rough stack a working version would use, and an honest no when AI is the wrong tool.
**What you do not get:** a roadmap, an architecture document, or any working code.

blocks.text: The €2,500-per-hour Big 4 partner is usually a slide reader. The €500-per-day independent engineer who ships LLMs every week is often better and ten times cheaper. Tier 1 is the right answer when you have a hunch about an AI use case and need an honest second opinion before sinking budget.
Tier 2: AI Readiness Audit and Roadmap (€2,500 to €25K, 2 to 4 weeks)

A structured engagement that produces a written AI readiness assessment, a prioritized list of use cases, a technical architecture recommendation, an implementation roadmap with milestones, and a final presentation for stakeholders. The deliverable is a written artifact your team can act on without the consultant in the room.
Most teams land in this tier. Companies past the workshop stage who know AI fits somewhere need someone to map the where, the how, and the what-not-to-build before committing budget.

The spread inside Tier 2 is real. A €25,000 audit from a generic strategy firm produces a deck filled with vendor logos and Gartner quadrants. A €2,500 audit from an engineering-led practice produces a working architecture sketch, named integration points, and a two-week pilot plan. Same tier on paper, opposite output.

Tier 3: Pilot Build with Production Proof-of-Concept (€25K to €75K, 4 to 10 weeks)

A working pilot. You hand over a real workflow, the consultant builds an end-to-end version with the code, the integrations, and the cost math, and your team operates it for 30 days under observation. The deliverable is working software plus an ROI report.

This is where most enterprise AI projects fail. Teams skip Tier 2, jump to a €60,000 pilot without scoping the data, and discover in week six that the source-of-truth database is three SAP exports glued together with VLOOKUPs. The pilot ships late, the ROI math collapses, and the next year's AI budget gets cut.
The right Tier 3 engagement starts with the Tier 2 artifact, not a kickoff workshop.

**Concrete example: MP Bau.** In late 2025, [webvise built a digital platform](/case-studies/mp-bau-construction) for Märkische Projekt Bau, a Brandenburg construction firm with 25 years of project history. The AI portion was a Gemini 2.5 Flash chatbot integrated into a multilingual Next.js site supporting eight languages. The full engagement shipped in 3 weeks at the bottom of this tier, with 95 Lighthouse Performance and sub 1.5-second page loads.

Without the prior Tier 1 conversation, the brief would have been 'add AI to our website'. With it, the brief was 'reduce response time on visitor queries about our project history'. That reframe is the difference between a working pilot and a museum chatbot nobody uses.
Tier 4: Enterprise AI Program (€75K to €300K+, 12 to 26 weeks)

Multi-team rollout with governance, training, and an in-house AI capability at the end. Typical scope: three to seven workflows automated, a model usage policy, security and compliance review, vendor selection across three to five categories, and a custody-of-data plan that holds up to GDPR scrutiny.

This tier sells. It also miscarries more than any other. The pattern is a procurement-led RFP, a Big 4 win at €175,000, six months of analyst hours producing decks, and a final presentation nobody in the engineering team can implement. Anthropic and OpenAI entering consulting at the top end is partly a response to this gap: the labs themselves are watching their model adoption stall on consultancies who cannot ship code.
What this tier should actually deliver: every roadmap line item has a named owner, a named model, a named integration, and a fixed-price build path. Anything less is a strategy poster.
What Hides Inside Each Tier Price
Two AI consulting quotes in the same tier can quote 8x apart. The spread comes down to four variables. Knowing them lets you compare proposals on substance instead of headline numbers.

items: **Who is in the room.** A partner-and-analyst team produces decks. An engineer-and-founder team produces architecture and code. Same tier, opposite output. Ask directly: who writes the Python.

**Deliverable depth.** A 'roadmap' can mean a six-line bulleted list or a 30-page architecture document with named models, named integrations, and a fixed-price build plan. Ask for a redacted sample before signing.

**Production handover.** Is the consultant gone on day 30, or is the team you trained working on the pilot? Honest engagements include a written handover and a 30-day support window. Cheap ones do not.

**Engineering bench depth.** A solo consultant with a Notion template costs the same as a small engineering-led practice that can also ship the build. The latter saves you the Tier 3 handoff cost. Ask whether the consultant can ship the work they are recommending, or only describe it.

blocks.text: The Buyer Mistake Most AI Pilots Make
The most common AI consulting failure is buying the wrong tier. Two patterns dominate.

**Pattern one: hiring Tier 4 when Tier 2 was the question.** A mid-size SaaS company with one well-defined use case (lead enrichment) signs a €150,000 enterprise AI program because their board wants 'AI strategy'. Six months later they have a deck and three vendor demos. The right answer was a €10,000 Tier 2 audit, a €40,000 Tier 3 pilot, and €100,000 of unused budget.

**Pattern two: hiring Tier 3 with no Tier 2 artifact.** A logistics firm commissions a €60,000 pilot to 'add AI to the dispatch workflow'. Week one, the consultant discovers the dispatch data lives in three systems with no canonical join. Week four, the pilot pivots to documentation cleanup. Week eight, the engagement closes with a working PoC for a workflow nobody asked for.

The corrective filter is honest: before signing a Tier 3 pilot, write down the use case in one paragraph, the data sources in three bullets, and the success metric in one number. If you cannot, your budget belongs in Tier 2 first. The math is covered in detail in our [AI automation ROI guide](/blog/ai-automation-roi-calculation).
How to Scope Your AI Consulting Engagement
Four filters get you to the right tier before you ask for quotes. Twenty minutes with your operations lead is enough.

items: **Filter 1: Do you have a named use case?** No means start in Tier 1 or Tier 2. Yes means consider Tier 3 directly.
**Filter 2: Is the data clean and accessible?** No means Tier 2 first, because data audit is part of the roadmap. Yes means jump to Tier 3.
**Filter 3: Do you have one workflow or seven?** One is Tier 2 plus Tier 3. Seven is Tier 4 territory, but only if the seven are sequenced, not parallel.

**Filter 4: Is the goal a slide deck or a working workflow?** A deck is Tier 1 or 2. A working workflow is Tier 3 minimum. If a Tier 3 vendor only produces a deck at the end, you bought a deck at pilot prices.

blocks.text: Four honest answers gets you to the right tier in one meeting. The discipline saves the typical AI buyer €40,000 to €90,000 of misallocated budget.
What to Skip Before Buying Any Tier

Skip a consulting engagement entirely when you already know the use case, the data is clean, and the only question is who will build it. That is an AI automation brief, not a consulting brief. Send it to a builder with a fixed-price quote and skip the strategy step.
Skip Tier 3 and 4 when you have no production data yet. A pilot on synthetic data ships a demo, not a workflow. Stay in Tier 1 or Tier 2 until the data exists.

Skip consulting entirely when your budget is under €2,500 and your team has the engineering muscle to read public frameworks. The Anthropic Cookbook, the Vercel AI SDK templates, and the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) reference servers cover most starter use cases. The right move is one engineer with two weeks, not a Tier 2 audit.
